answers.answer: No hard cycle on paper. Task 1.0's scenario validator precedes the compiler; Task 1.1 proves the checkpointer on a minimal graph independent of the compiler before 1.2 builds the compiler; Tasks 3–6 run against Task 1's test-only implementation registry until Task 7 registers the production factory-core implementations; Task 8 depends on Tasks 1–7; Task 13 depends on 8 and 11.1; Task 16 joins 13 and 15. The one soft circularity is the Common execution contract, which says each implementation slice receives an explicit delivery profile, run budget account and approved execution envelope, objects that exist only after Tasks 3–4. Read literally, the factory executes its own bootstrap.
answers.planImpact: In tasks.md Common execution contract, state that Tasks 1–8 execute under the M0 repository workflow with a manually recorded ledger (profile, envelope and budget as documentary records) and that the first factory-executed slice is Task 14's canary.
answers.evidence: tasks.md Task 1 (1.0–1.2, test-only implementation registry), Task 7 registrations, Task 8 Depends on, Common execution contract, Task 14; verify.md Wayfinding reconciliation checks (Task 1.0 first prerequisite).
answers.novelty: Questions 1–120 examined efficiency mechanisms; question 5 noted time-to-first-feedback but never tested prerequisite ordering.

answers.answer: Yes. Task 1.1 proves the pinned Bun/LangGraph/checkpointer interrupt/restart contract on a minimal graph with the SIGKILL resume test, forbids an in-memory saver in acceptance, and records go/no-go before 1.2. Its compatibility-refusal tests count against Task 1's own fixture worker/effect counters, and the task defers external-effect deduplication to Task 4 and the uncertain-effect upgrade fixture to Task 8. No K3s, ACP or BE is required. One ordering note: the application-store migration runner is extracted in Task 3.1, so Task 1's store-schema digest checks must use the checkpointer's own storage or a fixture store.
answers.planImpact: Preserve Task 1.1's independence from the compiler and from Tasks 3–6 and Task 1's restriction to the test-only registry; no reorder.

answers.novelty: Sharpens question 5 into whether the first slice is self-contained.

answers.answer: Only two of five. LangGraph persistence is a Task 1.1 go/no-go and OIDC is proven in Task 3.2 before Task 5 uses it. Live ACP capability (permission interception, resume, usage signals), K3s runtime-class isolation (gVisor/Kata probe, host preflight) and real provider usage reporting are first observed in Task 6, after Tasks 1–5 (about 70–145 estimated human hours). A09 already says to run authenticated adapter probes in the first execution slice, which the task order does not honor. The exposure is concrete: all three shipped profiles are enforcement strict with money caps, and the spec refuses strict admission without a defensible reservation and stop mechanism, so an adapter without usable usage and stop signals leaves every profile inadmissible. Task 6's stop rule exists but fires late.
answers.planImpact: Add Task 1 checkbox 1.3 beside 1.1: an authenticated, bounded ACP capability and usage-signal probe for the first provider, plus k3s-preflight and the runtime-class probe on the identified hosts, each recorded as go/no-go before Task 2; Task 6 keeps the full proofs.
answers.evidence: tasks.md Task 1.1, Task 3.2, Task 6 (6.1–6.3; Probe Claude first, then Codex; Probe gVisor first and Kata second); A09 revisit; A49 revisit; spec Capacity and budget admission scenario Telemetry is unavailable under a strict budget; execution.yaml profiles enforcement strict.
answers.novelty: Questions 1–120 assumed the integrations exist; none asked when their first evidence arrives.

answers.answer: Viable as a first store, with the gate already named. The design pins one active coordinator, a separate SQLite store and a restart-tested checkpointer with synchronous checkpointing; the serialized dispatch boundary ends at transport handoff so held remote responses cannot block it; Task 4.5 must measure scalingAcceptance.coordinator (64 sessions, 100 effects per second, p95 dispatch 100 ms) on an identified host; A08 names the reopen. Eight matrix workers sit well inside that budget. What the Twilight store does not inherit is the repository's recorded bun:sqlite landmine: WAL, busy_timeout and foreign_keys are asserted at open only in be-01 and the ESLint guard covers only apps/be-01/src, so a new app with two SQLite files plus an outbox is exposed to that fault again.
answers.planImpact: Task 3.1's extraction carries openConnection's pragma assertions and the bun:sqlite import lint into the shared library so apps/twilight-be and the checkpointer use them; Task 4.5's evidence records the host's storage and fsync characteristics.
answers.evidence: design.md Durable execution and effect ownership, States, attempts and leases (serialized boundary); execution.yaml scalingAcceptance.coordinator; tasks.md Task 3.1, Task 4.5; A08; LLM_README.md Landmines (bun:sqlite).
answers.novelty: Questions 31–36 treated durability as given; store viability was not asked.

answers.answer: Yes, several are not gated. M1 requires one dedicated K3s server and two agent nodes on hosts other than h3mon and h4claw, none identified; Task 6 says infrastructure spending needs an explicit allowance but names no readiness gate for acquiring them. Worker images are digest-pinned, but the build and publish path (Dagger on h2puni to the self-hosted registry) and the agent nodes' pull credentials and reachability are preconditions nowhere. Provider accounts and quota for eight concurrent sessions in 8.4 are reported as constraints, not gated. The M1 FE journey needs an operator OIDC issuer binding (A30: absent config refuses startup) beyond Task 3.2's local test issuer, and the h3mon export sink is assumed. k3s-preflight covers host compatibility only.
answers.planImpact: Extend Task 6.2's k3s-preflight and runbook into the M1 readiness gate: identified hosts with allowance, registry reachability and pull credentials from agent nodes, provider accounts and quota for 8.4's concurrency, the operator OIDC issuer binding and the h3mon sink; Task 8.1 and 8.4 cite it as an entry condition.

answers.novelty: Question 76 treated quota as a benchmark confound; hardware, DNS and issuer readiness were never asked.

answers.answer: Partly. Human wait is its own interval kind, human minutes are explicit, paused decisions hold no worker, one decision approves plan plus envelope, and the focus profile batches decisions; 8.4 reports human and queue wait in its percentiles. What is unmeasured is the operator's decision load on the acceptance proofs themselves: beforeStage.implementation requires a human decision per run, decision tokens are browser-only, and 8.4 runs three workloads at four capacities for five repetitions, so the operator may have to mint on the order of sixty to a few hundred approvals by hand. The plan neither says how those approvals are supplied nor reports decision count and wait share.
answers.planImpact: Task 8.4 states the approval mechanism for the matrix (one human-approved envelope covering the fixed requests per capacity point, as A03 permits) and reports decision count, operator minutes and human-wait share of elapsed; Task 13's acceptance reports the same.
answers.evidence: design.md Budget accounts and clocks (Human minutes), Human decisions; execution.yaml policies.beforeStage.implementation, scalingAcceptance; tasks.md Task 8.4; A03; product-experience.md Focus profile.
answers.novelty: Question 104 asked whether optimizations shift cost to humans; this asks whether the operator is the unmeasured critical path of acceptance itself.

Under factory-core the accepted outcome is candidate-accepted-at-handoff; staging, cloud acceptance, publication and dev-main record inapplicable dispositions and the spec says no source or environment changes. So the run yields a verified but unpublished candidate that reaches main only by the operator's manual merge until Task 13. The heading Accept the first useful factory run invites the broader reading the text forbids.

answers.answer: Not on the plan's own terms. Every task carries human-hour, agent-hour and token ranges, but the plan withholds the sum (no aggregate completion date is asserted; M1 duration remains unmeasured). Adding the personal-loop ranges for Tasks 1–8, 11, 13, 15 and 16 gives roughly 280–560 human hours and 3–9 million tokens before benchmark, infrastructure and provider spend, which is the figure the operator needs to judge viability and which nothing in the manifest states. A re-estimate checkpoint after Tasks 1–4 already exists.

answers.answer: Recovery point is implied but unstated: synchronous checkpointing plus the outbox make it the last committed transition. Recovery time is stated nowhere for Twilight's own store; only planning storage has a restart reconciliation budget, and A68's release window is unrelated. For one operator a numeric RTO promise would be premature (the A53 pattern), but the expectation should be explicit and measured rather than absent.

answers.answer: Largely yes for grants, partly for raw secrets. Authority intersects current grants, revocation and floors at admission and again at dispatch; Task 3.3 revokes membership, repository, approval and integration grants while work is queued; Task 4.2 revokes between intent and dispatch; A34 destroys the credential mount after observed exit and revokes short-lived grants where supported. Decision tokens are server-side records, so no signing key exists to rotate. The uncovered case is a provider secret rotated in the secret store while an attempt still holds the old value in its mount: tests cover expired and revoked credentials, not rotation mid-attempt, and the direct provider call is not brokered.
answers.planImpact: Add to Task 6.3's credential lifecycle tests: rotate the repository/provider secret while an attempt is live, assert the next brokered dispatch revalidates the integration grant, the run view shows the stale mount, and the old value never reaches a new attempt.

A49 and ADR 0016 fix one dedicated server that schedules no attempt Pods; the design says losing it pauses new launch and stop commands visibly and reconciles recorded attempts after declarative rebootstrap; the spec scenario The K3s server is lost and reconstructed and Tasks 6.2 and 8.4 exercise API loss, node loss and rebootstrap. No HA claim exists to disguise. The coordinator on h4claw is likewise a single failure domain by design.

FE and MCP call the same BE operations; OpenClaw enters through one authenticated Twilight operation and is not a second delivery coordinator; Task 5 delivers run view, pause/resume/cancel/retry/skip and the recovery inbox before Task 15 exists; Task 15's exit requires unavailable secretary capacity to be reported rather than answered and a general request to create no run. The residual shared fate is that h4claw hosts both OpenClaw and Twilight's control services, a host failure domain (question 135), not an assistant dependency.

answers.answer: Mostly. Each run retains a compatibility manifest (controller/graph, compiler, Bun/lock digest, serializer/saver, store schema, hook and adapter digests); restoreRun refuses incompatible closures; migrations are additive with down.sql; a later workflow or floor publication never changes an existing run; Task 8.3 rehearses refusal and Task 14 proves migration and rollback per supported path. The gap is the worker image: Jobs carry a digest, but it is not in the run's manifest or profile epoch, so a retry after an image upgrade could run on a different image without a recorded compatibility change.

Defaults are explicit (no-age-expiry corpus under a 10 GiB ceiling; operational evidence 365 days after the terminal transition), but Task 7.2 persists evidence and traces without recording retention class or measuring bytes, the ceiling and export path are Task 16 work, no task owns the 365-day expiry job, and durable records (events, outbox, ledger) have no bound at all. Between Task 7 and Task 16 the scaling matrix alone generates sixty runs of traces on hosts with unstated disk.

answers.answer: Partly. Telemetry loss is modeled as unavailable, never zero capacity or a healthy worker (Tasks 5.3, 6.2); the efficiency breakdown does not reserve, authorize or reprice; evidence producers are floor failures when unavailable, which correctly blocks acceptance. But resolve_effect requires evidence references, so an evidence-store outage while an effect is unknown could block the only recovery path, and the grill's question 36 recommendation to protect cancellation and reconciliation from optional consumers has no named test in Task 4.

Fallback is bounded to the declared ladder, quota and provisioning failures are visible constraints, unknown spend retains its hold, and a provider outside the envelope needs a new decision. But the escalation vocabulary is refusal, gateFailure and blockingFinding; a provider outage or timeout is none of these, so an attempt failing for that reason has no defined disposition: it could consume a rework round or ladder step, or fail the activity with no operator action named.

answers.answer: Yes, because authority is not clock-derived. Leases carry a fencing token; the coordinator's serialized dispatch boundary decides staleness by fence and current authority; expiry withdraws authority and proves nothing about the process; approval, decision-token and deadline expiry are evaluated on the coordinator's clock from persisted createdAt. Worker and provider clocks affect only observations (K3s active deadline, cleanup TTL, provider timestamps recorded as-of). k3s-preflight checks clock at install.
answers.planImpact: Preserve fence-based authority in dispatchEffect and Task 4.2's fence faults; no clock-synchronization requirement is needed for authority.

answers.answer: Yes, forever, and nobody can release it. Each reservation needs resource-specific terminal evidence; missing or unreadable remote state retains the hold; resolve_effect's three dispositions settle the effect outcome only, and Task 4.2 says abandon_unknown does not release a still-active remote reservation. With buildSlots 1 and browserSlots 1, one provider job whose terminal state can never be read blocks every later build or browser activity, and cancelling the run releases only proven-free reservations.

Source writes occur only in an attempt's isolated workspace; discovery artifacts live in a draft workspace and content-addressed storage until published; composition happens in an isolated workspace; publication is a compare-and-swap on the accepted ref and a moved base triggers recomposition. The operator's own checkout is never a Twilight write target; outside planning edits are imported as proposals and quarantined if divergent; dirty work requires a content manifest.

answers.answer: Sufficient for the stated design, because it never asks the three stores to commit together. Twilight stores immutable PlanRefs, not plans; progress and completion receipts are broker commands with stable idempotency keys; the broker publishes events only after acceptance, a repeated command returns its prior answer, and on crash it rereads the accepted ref and journal. That is the same outbox-and-idempotency pattern the coordinator uses between its own store and checkpointer, and Task 9's exit tests include restart-before-acknowledgement replay.
answers.planImpact: Preserve ADR 0015 and protocol step 4; each broker command from Twilight is an effect with recorded intent under dispatchEffect, which the effect contract already requires for brokered writes.

Cutover is shadow-read, verified backup, short write freeze, canonical comparison, backend switch, with no dual-write period; rollback after new Git writes replays them into the old backend during a freeze. Native Backlog tools edit materialized candidate views that must import through the broker, so they are proposal inputs, not a second authority, and the generated tasks.md is drift-checked in CI. answers.answer: Stop, pause and inspect yes; recover no. command_run (pause, resume, cancel, retry, skip), get_run, list_run_events and get_capacity are MCP operations, so any authenticated MCP client works when the FE is broken. But approval, resolve_effect and release require the same human decision capability, decision tokens are minted only by the browser flow (POST /api/decision-tokens is browser only), and the only browser-free trusted path is the protected recovery command for upgrade rollback. A broken FE therefore blocks resolving an unknown effect or releasing.

structured_output.verdict: Feasible as a document-backed contract, not yet viable to execute as written. On paper the plan has no prerequisite cycle, proves durable restart first, models its single failure domains, preserves workspace and publication isolation, keeps planning authority atomic, and genuinely defers customer scope. Four things keep it short of viable: the highest-risk external evidence (live ACP capability, provider usage signals, K3s runtime isolation, host and credential readiness) arrives only at Task 6; the personal-loop cost is unsummed and has no program-level stop rule; several checkboxes hide multi-week batches; and four operational gaps have no owner (routine backup and restore, recovery when evidence storage is down, permanently held reservations, and a browser-only decision path). Nothing in the manifest is runtime evidence, and no answer here is a human approval.
